idiom_name: ScalaFX properties over JavaFX; immutable case-class screen state as the functional alternative
implementation_notes: ScalaFX is the Scala UI DSL over JavaFX (the project describes itself that way and versions track JavaFX releases), so the presentation model can use the inherited Property/Binding machinery: a state holder with ObjectProperty/BooleanProperty fields that the view binds, testable without a stage. Scala's own idiom pulls the other way: screen state as an immutable case class whose copy method produces the next state, commands as methods returning that state, and a view that re-renders from it - the case-class documentation notes parameters are vals and instances compare by structure. Take the ScalaFX route when JavaFX bindings are wanted; take the case-class route when the screen is a pure function of state and equality-friendly testing matters more than declarative binding.
code_sketch:
final case class LoginState(email: String = "", busy: Boolean = false):
  def submitEnabled: Boolean = email.nonEmpty && !busy   // decision
  def submitted: LoginState = copy(busy = true)          // command -> next state

// view: render(state); field.onChange = e => state = state.copy(email = e)
pitfalls: ScalaFX releases are tied to JavaFX and JDK versions (the README maps both and requires a recent JDK for the newest releases), so a mismatched toolchain fails at startup with module errors.
JavaFX properties are mutable reference cells while case classes are values: mixing the two creates two sources of truth unless one is clearly authoritative.
A var in a case class undermines copy/equality semantics - keep property-based holders as classes and immutable state as case classes, not a blend.
Case-class updates allocate a new state per interaction; on hot paths this feeds the JVM's GC pressure, which is why some screens cache derived values.
